X-Reset: Scaling Object-Centric Reinforcement Learning via Cross-Embodiment Resets

Prithwish Dan Affiliation: Applied Intuition, Mountain View, CA, USA , Chenyang Ma Affiliation: Applied Intuition, Mountain View, CA, USA and Wei Zhan Affiliation: Applied Intuition, Mountain View, CA, USA
2026
Abstract.

Reinforcement learning (RL) in simulation can train dexterous manipulation policies without robot demonstrations, but training a single generalist policy with task-agnostic rewards faces a severe exploration problem: approaching, grasping, and reorienting diverse objects with many degrees of freedom is difficult to discover from scratch. Prior works make exploration tractable with high-quality robot demonstrations, per-task reward shaping, or by restricting policies to narrow modes of behavior. We propose X-Reset, a framework that instead resolves exploration with human hand-object demonstrations. Rather than imitating or tracking retargeted human motion, X-Reset kinematically retargets hand-object states to noisy robot states, filters out states that are unstable in simulation, and samples the remainder as resets during RL training with general-purpose object-centric rewards. The resulting policy depends only on object state and goal, with demonstrations entering training through the reset distribution. We show that X-Reset trains generalist policies on 20 objects across three embodiments—a 22-DoF hand on two different arms and a parallel-jaw gripper—and resolves the exploration challenges of RL from scratch. X-Reset scales with the number of training objects, generalizes to unseen objects, can learn from imperfect hand-pose estimates, and transfers behaviors zero-shot from sim-to-real.

1. Introduction

The predominant recipe for training robot manipulation policies is imitation learning (IL), in which robot data is used as supervision to learn a mapping from observations to actions (Chi et al., 2023; Black et al., 2025). Scaling such approaches to general-purpose models faces the fundamental bottleneck of requiring large-scale datasets of high-quality expert demonstrations (Lin et al., 2024). Despite a multitude of collection systems (Chi et al., 2024; Handa et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2024; Arunachalam et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2023; Iyer et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024), teleoperation remains most expensive precisely where dexterity matters most: multi-fingered hands with many degrees of freedom (DoF). Reinforcement learning (RL) in simulation offers an alternative that requires no robot demonstrations, and has produced dexterous skills that transfer to the real world (OpenAI et al., 2019; Handa et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023).

However, RL faces a large exploration burden when learning to approach, grasp, and reorient objects with many DoF from scratch, and prior works make the problem tractable with per-task scaffolding or restricted behavior. Demonstration-led curricula (Bauza et al., 2025; Tao et al., 2024) and favorable reset distributions (Yin et al., 2026) reduce this burden but require high-quality robot demonstrations or hand-designed per-task states. Recent works that train generalist object-centric RL controllers instead mitigate exploration by learning only narrow modes of behavior, such as operating only on tool handles (Kedia et al., 2026) or strictly learning top-down power grasps via reward shaping (Kuang et al., 2026). We instead aim to train a single generalist policy to learn these skills on a diverse set of objects with a task-agnostic reward.

Human videos, which are abundant and encompass a diverse range of day-to-day hand-object interactions (Damen et al., 2022; Hoque et al., 2025; Chao et al., 2021), are a natural source of guidance for this exploration problem. Many works use human data directly for imitation by kinematically retargeting hand motion to robot actions (Qin et al., 2022; Lepert et al., 2025; Lepert et al., 2026), but retargeting is only a rough estimate of robot motion and often fails to obey the true contact dynamics of robot-object interaction. Works that use RL to bridge the embodiment gap either transfer human object motion to train single-task policies (Dan et al., 2025; Lum et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2024) or use retargeted motion as a reference for RL (Guzey et al., 2024; Zhu et al., 2026; Mandi et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025), often relying on high-quality MoCap data and restricting learned behaviors to specifically demonstrated strategies. Our key insight is that kinematically retargeted human hand-object states can supplement RL with task-agnostic rewards by offering a natural reset distribution of states from which robots can easily explore and access success signals during training. Resetting to reference states is standard practice in humanoid motion tracking (Peng et al., 2018; Luo et al., 2023), where the policy is conditioned on and rewarded for following the reference. For general-purpose manipulation, direct reference-tracking is under-specified under important randomizations such as novel goal poses and external forces that may knock objects into unseen states (Lum et al., 2026); our policy instead depends only on object state and goal, and demonstrations enter training only through resets.

We propose X-Reset, a framework to train dexterous manipulation policies by defining reset distributions over human hand-object states during RL training (Fig. 1). X-Reset kinematically retargets hand-object trajectories to the target embodiment, filters out states that are unstable in simulation, and randomly resets to the retained states while training object-centric RL to approach, grasp, and reorient objects. These resets allow quicker access to success signals that are otherwise difficult to discover from scratch. Our contributions are summarized as follows:

  1. (1)

    We propose X-Reset, a framework that makes task-agnostic object-centric RL tractable for dexterous manipulation by framing human hand-object states as a reset distribution to remedy the exploration problem.

  2. (2)

    We show that X-Reset trains generalist RL policies on 20 DexYCB (Chao et al., 2021) objects with task-agnostic rewards. Across three embodiments—a five-fingered hand on two different arms and a parallel-jaw gripper—average reorientation success increases from 11.0%11.0\% to 66.6%66.6\% with object-only rewards, and from 42.1%42.1\% to 59.6%59.6\% with hand-object rewards.

  3. (3)

    We show that X-Reset scales with the number of training objects, generalizes zero-shot to unseen objects, and serves as a base policy for fine-tuning on novel objects without additional human demonstrations. X-Reset is also robust to offline hand-pose estimation errors at training time, and learned behaviors transfer zero-shot from simulation to the real world for a 22-DoF hand mounted on a 6-DoF arm on both seen and unseen objects.

2. Related Work

Dexterous Manipulation with RL. RL in simulation has produced dexterous skills that transfer to the real world (OpenAI et al., 2019; Handa et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023), but exploration is a major bottleneck when training high-DoF hands from scratch. Demonstration-based initialization and curricula reduce this burden (Florensa et al., 2017; Bauza et al., 2025; Tao et al., 2024) but need high-quality robot data; OmniReset (Yin et al., 2026) instead trains single-task policies from manually specified reset distributions for parallel-jaw grippers. Generalist controllers also exploit structured priors: (Kedia et al., 2026; Lum et al., 2026) target handle-like tools using a shared grasp-region representation and reports that PPO alone is insufficient for exploration, while (Kuang et al., 2026) combines object-keypoint rewards with finger-curl shaping and learns only top-down power grasps. X-Reset retains a generic object-centric reward and instead addresses exploration through the reset distribution, sourced from diverse human data rather than expensive robot data, and can learn behaviors on diverse objects ranging from scissors to bowls to powerdrills.

Reference State Initialization. Reference state initialization is standard in motion tracking for humanoids (Peng et al., 2018; Luo et al., 2023) where the training objective explicitly rewards reference-following. Works in manipulation (Li et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025) use kinematic imitation rewards to shape exploration and reference-following, relying on MoCap data for accurate hand-object pose and contact estimation (Mandi et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025). Reference-tracking for contact-rich manipulation faces diversity challenges, since there is no natural hand-object reference to imitate under important randomizations (Lum et al., 2026) such as novel goal poses or external forces which may knock objects over. Instead, our approach does not require tracking the reference at every step; it injects noisy retargeted resets to supplement object-centric RL training of policies which simply consume current object state and goal.

Learning from Human Hand-Object Data. Human videos offer a scalable source of object-interaction priors (Grauman et al., 2022; Hoque et al., 2025; Chao et al., 2021), but lack the action labels needed for standard IL. To bridge this, prior work maps human motion to robot actions through kinematic retargeting (Qin et al., 2022; Shaw et al., 2022; Li et al., 2024; Qiu et al., 2025), narrows the visual gap by overlaying rendered robot arms on human frames (Lepert et al., 2025; Lepert et al., 2026; Lepert et al., 2024) or unifying both into a shared keypoint representation (Ren et al., 2025; Haldar and Pinto, 2025; Pace et al., 2025), or decouples video-derived planning from low-level control (Li et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2023; Shi et al., 2025). These methods assume retargeted hand motions can be directly imitated on the robot, but this often fails due to embodiment mismatch and the true contact dynamics of robot-object interaction (Dan et al., 2025), and they typically require co-training with substantial robot data to recover. Human-guided RL instead uses residual actions or motion/contact references (Guzey et al., 2024; Zhu et al., 2026; Mandi et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025), or guides learning through object trajectories and hand-derived initialization (Dan et al., 2025; Lum et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2024), typically producing single-task policies. X-Reset uses human data neither as an imitation target nor as a per-task reference, but as a reset distribution for a single generalist policy.

3. Problem Formulation

We focus on the problem of learning the core dexterous manipulation skills—approaching, grasping, and reorienting objects to goal poses—via object-centric RL in simulation, with reset states from diverse human demonstrations. For a given object η\eta, a human hand-object trajectory ξη={(ht,st)}t=1T\xi^{\eta}=\{(h_{t},s_{t})\}_{t=1}^{T} consists of TT densely tracked timesteps of MANO (Romero et al., 2017) hand poses where ht∈ℝK×3h_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times 3} represents the 3D position of each of the K=21K=21 hand keypoints and st∈SE⁡(3)s_{t}\in\mathrm{SE(3)} represents the position and rotation of the object at timestep tt. We define the goal pose g=sTg=s_{T} as the last object pose from the human demonstration. In practice, we represent object poses by sampling Z=64Z=64 keypoints on the object surface to enable a richer geometric representation: stkp,gkp∈ℝZ×3s_{t}^{\rm kp},g^{\rm kp}\in\mathbb{R}^{Z\times 3}. We denote a dataset of NN human hand-object trajectories 𝒟η={ξiη}i=1N\mathcal{D}^{\eta}=\{\xi_{i}^{\eta}\}_{i=1}^{N}, and construct a dataset of many objects 𝒟=⋃η𝒟η\mathcal{D}=\bigcup_{\eta}\mathcal{D}^{\eta}. We learn a policy to produce actions 𝐚t=πϕ​(qt,stkp,gkp,mt)\mathbf{a}_{t}=\pi_{\phi}(q_{t},s_{t}^{\rm kp},g^{\rm kp},m_{t}) given robot proprioception qtq_{t}, object keypoints stkps_{t}^{\rm kp}, goal keypoints gkpg^{\rm kp}, and LSTM state mtm_{t} encoding the interaction history; ϕ\phi denotes the learned policy parameters.

4. Approach

We propose X-Reset, which consists of two primary stages: (1) generating robot reset states from human hand-object poses; (2) training RL policies in simulation with object-centric rewards by incorporating random resets to demonstrated states to remedy the exploration problem.

4.1. Generating Reset States from Human Hand-Object Demonstrations

We first generate reset states for the robot from human demonstrations (Fig. 2, Top). Such states must consist of (a) joint configurations for the robot, and (b) the 6D object pose and goal, so that they can be spawned into simulation (NVIDIA, 2026).

Hand-Object Data Processing. We employ an optimization-based kinematic retargeting pipeline (using PyRoki (Kim et al., 2025)) to estimate robot joint angles corresponding to each frame of the human demonstration. We first convert human hand pose ht∈ℝK×3h_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times 3} to robot hand joint angles θthand\theta_{t}^{\mathrm{hand}} using approximate fingertip and wrist keypoint targets following prior work (Mandi et al., 2025). Then, we perform collision-aware inverse kinematics (using cuRobo (Sundaralingam et al., 2023)) to solve for the remaining arm joints θtarm\theta_{t}^{\mathrm{arm}} by tracking the wrist over time while keeping the hand poses fixed to finally obtain θt∈ℝJ\theta_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{J} where JJ is the number of joints in the target embodiment. This process allows us to generate a dataset of LL hand-object pairs for the robot 𝒟robot={(θl,sl)}l=1L\mathcal{D}_{\rm robot}=\{(\theta_{l},s_{l})\}_{l=1}^{L}.

Filtering Unstable Resets. In practice, kinematic retargeting from human to robot hand can result in unrealistic states depending on the embodiment gap. To avoid sampling unstable simulation resets, we perform offline filtering to mark and discard hand-object states which are undesirable. These may be a byproduct of (i) failure to find robot joint configurations within joint limits or (ii) instability when spawned in simulation (e.g., due to hand-object penetration).

4.2. Supplementing Object-Centric Reinforcement Learning with Simulation Resets

Next, we perform RL training with generic object-centric reward functions to train robots to manipulate objects to goal poses (Fig. 2, Bottom). Key to our approach is the use of simulation resets: over the course of training, we occasionally reset to hand-object states generated in Section 4.1. By exposing the policy to diverse resets that lie in high-value regions, success signals from later stages of manipulation propagate and help avoid the collapse to local optima often faced by naive exploration from scratch.

Object-Centric Reward Function. We adopt a standard object-centric reward function for training RL policies which is common across all objects and robot policies:

(1) rt=rprox​(qt,stkp)+𝟙prox​rreorient​(stkp,gkp)+𝟙prox​rsuccess​(stkp,gkp)+rsmooth​(𝐚t)+rsafety\begin{split}r_{t}={}&r_{\rm prox}(q_{t},s_{t}^{\rm kp})+\mathds{1}_{\rm prox}r_{\rm reorient}(s_{t}^{\rm kp},g^{\rm kp})\\ &+\mathds{1}_{\rm prox}r_{\rm success}(s_{t}^{\rm kp},g^{\rm kp})+r_{\rm smooth}(\mathbf{a}_{t})+r_{\rm safety}\end{split}

The proximity reward rproxr_{\rm prox} encourages the robot hand to approach the object, while the reorientation reward rreorientr_{\rm reorient} drives the object toward its goal pose. rsuccessr_{\rm success} provides an additional bonus for achieving the goal pose within an ϵ\epsilon threshold, and rsmoothr_{\rm smooth} encourages smooth and small actions. Finally, rsafetyr_{\rm safety} penalizes terminal failures such as the object leaving the workspace or sustained contact between the robot and the table.

In practice, there are various metrics to measure the distance between the current object pose sts_{t} and goal pose gg in order to compute rreorientr_{\rm reorient}. Based on prior work (Kuang et al., 2026; Kedia et al., 2026), we compute the mean distance between corresponding keypoints:

(2) dkp​(stkp,gkp)=1Z​∑z=1Z‖st,zkp−gzkp‖2,rreorient∝−dkpd_{\rm kp}(s_{t}^{\rm kp},g^{\rm kp})=\frac{1}{Z}\sum_{z=1}^{Z}\left\|s_{t,z}^{\rm kp}-g_{z}^{\rm kp}\right\|_{2},\qquad r_{\rm reorient}\propto-d_{\rm kp}

This distance jointly captures differences in object position and orientation.

Resetting to Hand-Object States. At initialization, each environment is assigned an object and a demonstration for that object. We define the default reset distribution of the robot and object as ρdefault\rho_{\rm default} (including randomizations in start and goal poses), and ρdemo\rho_{\rm demo} as a uniform distribution over the retained frames of its assigned demonstration, using the corresponding retargeted hand-object states from 𝒟robot\mathcal{D}_{\rm robot}. At train time, we sample resets from ρdefault\rho_{\rm default} with probability 1−p1-p and sample from ρdemo\rho_{\rm demo} with probability pp. This reset scheme helps expose the policy πϕ\pi_{\phi} to a diverse set of states in simulation which lie along noisy robot trajectories and can enable discovery of success signals otherwise inaccessible via naive exploration from ρdefault\rho_{\rm default}.

Policy Details. We train our policy using PPO (Schulman et al., 2017). Our policy consumes the current and goal object keypoints and robot proprioception. The LSTM architecture consumes the interaction history and enables adaptive behaviors. We also leverage an asymmetric critic (Pinto et al., 2018) that has access to additional privileged information to further stabilize training. We apply standard domain randomization and object/robot perturbations inspired by prior work (Kedia et al., 2026; Lum et al., 2026). The policy can be deployed directly in the real world using vision foundation models to track object pose (see Section 5.4).

5. Experiments

Experimental Setup. We evaluate three embodiments: a 22-DoF Sharpa right hand on a 6-DoF UR7e arm, the same hand on a 7-DoF KUKA iiwa 14 arm, and a 1-DoF Robotiq 2F-85 parallel-jaw gripper on a UR7e arm. We train a separate generalist policy for each embodiment. We use hand-object trajectories from DexYCB (Chao et al., 2021) and IsaacSim (NVIDIA, 2026) for physics simulation. Unless otherwise specified, each policy is jointly trained on 20 objects with 20 right-handed demonstrations per object, and X-Reset uses p=0.9p=0.9 as the probability of sampling hand-object resets from ρdemo\rho_{\rm demo}. We train every simulation condition with three seeds.

Evaluation Metrics. In simulation, our primary task metric is Reorientation Success (%), which measures whether the object reaches its goal pose within a keypoint error of ϵ=2​cm\epsilon=2\,\mathrm{cm} under the distance metric dkpd_{\rm kp} in Section 4.2. We additionally measure Avg. Episode Return from ρdefault\rho_{\rm default} to compare training dynamics across policies on a common state distribution. Simulation results report means over three seeds, with standard errors shown in the figures. We aim to answer the following questions:

  1. (1)

    Cross-Embodiment Resets: Does X-Reset resolve the exploration problem faced by object-centric RL from scratch, and how does it compare against baselines on functionally retargeting human demonstrations?

  2. (2)

    Scaling and Generalization: What are X-Reset’s scaling and generalization properties when manipulating unseen objects without human demonstrations?

  3. (3)

    Reset Distribution: How does the probability of sampling hand-object states affect training behavior?

  4. (4)

    Real-World Capabilities: Can X-Reset learn from noisy offline hand tracking and transfer behaviors from sim-to-real under object-tracking noise?

5.1. Cross-Embodiment Resets

We evaluate whether X-Reset’s hand-object resets make object-centric RL tractable across embodiments. This comparison uses the demonstrated object start/goal pairs from DexYCB (20 per object). We compare against direct kinematic playback and two dominant reward-family baselines.

  • •

    Kinematic Retargeting: Used as the foundational backbone for prior works that perform Imitation Learning (IL) from human hand actions (Lepert et al., 2026; Haldar and Pinto, 2025; Ren et al., 2025), this baseline defines a kinematic mapping between 3D MANO hand positions (Romero et al., 2017) and robot joints. Robot arm and hand joint angles are then solved for via Inverse Kinematics (IK) (Section 4.1), and rolled out open-loop.

  • •

    Obj-Only Reward: The generic object-keypoint reward of Section 4.2, following the task-agnostic formulation of generalist controllers (Kedia et al., 2026; Kuang et al., 2026). rreorientr_{\text{reorient}} drives the object toward its goal and rproxr_{\text{prox}} encourages the hand to approach the object surface.

  • •

    Hand-Obj Reward: Adds hand guidance inspired by reference-tracking works (Mandi et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025). It shapes rproxr_{\text{prox}} to encourage robot fingertips to lie near the human fingertips at the demonstrated goal pose, and remains well-defined under perturbed object states by anchoring relative to the object itself.

We group the 20 objects into 7 Easy, 7 Medium, and 6 Hard objects based on learnability for baselines, trending from simple to complex geometries (Fig. 3). Kinematic Retargeting struggles to establish stable grasps due to the human-robot embodiment gap, with an average reorientation success of only 4.9%4.9\% across the three embodiments. Obj-Only Reward struggles with naive exploration, reaching 15.0%15.0\% average success on Easy objects and 11.0%11.0\% overall. Hand-Obj Reward benefits from hand-guided shaping and reaches 42.1%42.1\% average success overall.

Applying X-Reset to both reward structures improves performance across all three embodiments (Fig. 3). Averaged over objects and embodiments, reorientation success increases from 11.0%11.0\% to 66.6%66.6\% for Obj-Only Reward and from 42.1%42.1\% to 59.6%59.6\% for Hand-Obj Reward. Obj-Only Reward+X-Reset achieves a higher success rate despite the lower starting performance of its from-scratch baseline. These results support the general recipe: X-Reset to seed exploration, and Obj-Only Rewards with minimal bias and high freedom to explore robust embodiment-specific strategies instead of explicitly rewarding closeness to the human demos.

5.2. Scaling and Generalization

We evaluate Obj-Only Reward+X-Reset’s ability to transfer to unseen objects as we vary the number of training objects. We train UR7e+Sharpa policies on a range of 1-20 DexYCB objects and evaluate zero-shot reorientation on a fixed set of 12 objects from EBench (InternRobotics, 2026), with four objects per difficulty category (Fig. 4). We evaluate each object over 400 trials with varying start/goal conditions. Increasing training diversity improves transfer overall: on Easy objects, which share more familiar geometries with the training data, success starts high and rises from 64.8%64.8\% to 89.6%89.6\%. On Hard objects, including a very large bowl and a thin fork, we improve from 16.8%16.8\% to 43.5%43.5\%.

We also study X-Reset’s adaptability under a matched 10k-epoch budget: 5k epochs of DexYCB pretraining followed by 5k EBench epochs (Fine-tuned), versus 10k EBench epochs from random initialization (Scratch). Both policies train on the same 12 EBench objects. Because the assets have no corresponding human demonstrations, both EBench training segments use default resets (p=0p=0). Fine-tuning reaches 85.9%85.9\% average reorientation success, compared to just 39.1%39.1\% from scratch. X-Reset therefore also serves as an initialization for adapting to novel objects without new human demonstrations.

5.3. Reset Distribution

We ablate Obj-Only Reward+X-Reset’s training behavior on UR7e+Sharpa as we vary pp, the probability of sampling resets from ρdemo\rho_{\rm demo} (Fig. 5). We analyze Avg. Episode Return from ρdefault\rho_{\rm default} to fairly compare all policies. Early in training, higher sampling rates of hand-object states accelerate learning. As training converges, X-Reset policies reach returns between 55.4555.45 and 61.0961.09, all substantially outperforming the 0%0\% condition at 8.288.28. The benefit therefore holds over a broad range of sampling probabilities, rather than depending on p=0.9p=0.9 specifically.

5.4. Real-World Capabilities

Learning from Noisy Hand Poses. Since DexYCB estimates hand and object pose from privileged multi-view cameras, we inject varying levels of noise into the hand poses to test whether policies still learn from imperfect offline data. We add random wrist noise that translates the whole hand, plus per-keypoint finger noise. We perturb the same clean hand poses at each noise level, then apply kinematic retargeting and the instability filtering in Section 4.1. Fig. 6 shows the noisy human poses, corresponding robot configurations, and Avg. Episode Return for UR7e+Sharpa with Obj-Only Reward. Compared to a return of 58.5358.53 with clean poses, the noisy conditions reach 51.4651.46–56.0756.07, again well above the 8.288.28 obtained from exploration without demonstration resets. The High-noise condition also has a 2.45×2.45\times higher reset rejection rate than Clean (6.82% to 16.71%), which may explain some of the degradation in performance. Still, a generic object-centric reward is useful here: noisy hand estimates enter training only through resets, whereas in reference-tracking methods (Mandi et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025) the same noise would corrupt the imitation target itself.

Sim-to-Real Transfer. The actor uses robot proprioception and object-centric observations available through a vision pipeline, while the asymmetric critic receives additional simulation information. We reconstruct object meshes with SAM 3D (SAM 3D Team et al., 2025), track poses with FoundationPose (Wen et al., 2024), and sample surface keypoints. We deploy the UR7e+Sharpa policy on seen (Mustard ∈\in DexYCB) and unseen (Pringles, Hammer ∉\notin DexYCB) on a range of start and goal poses. The policy successfully transfers behaviors to the real hardware; the table in Fig. 7 reports the per-object results. Qualitatively, the policy also shows recovery behavior and robustness to perturbation, for example sliding fingers underneath the Mustard when it is slipping (Fig. 7, Top Left). The primary observed failure mode is object-pose estimation error, motivating future visual or visuo-tactile policy distillation.

6. Discussion and Limitations

We present X-Reset, which trains generalist dexterous manipulation policies by using retargeted human hand-object states as a reset distribution for object-centric RL. Resets make task-agnostic rewards tractable where exploration from scratch fails, and the resulting policies scale with training objects, tolerate noisy hand tracking, and transfer zero-shot to hardware.

Limitations. Consuming object pose makes the policy inherit tracking noise; visual (Dan et al., 2025; Yin et al., 2026) or visuo-tactile distillation (Lee et al., 2026) is a natural remedy, and can be combined with high-level planners to execute long-horizon as a sequence of goal-reaching subtasks (Kedia et al., 2026; Kuang et al., 2026). We also have yet to scale to large egocentric datasets (Hoque et al., 2025; Damen et al., 2022), which would require real-to-sim pipelines that extract hand-object states from video for rigid, articulated, and deformable objects.

Appendix A Implementation and Evaluation Details

A.1. Data and Representation

DexYCB (Chao et al., 2021; Romero et al., 2017) supplies synchronized MANO keypoints, object poses, and meshes. A common table-aligned transform maps each demonstration’s hand and object into simulation; robot-base transforms map wrist targets into arm coordinates. We sample 64 ordered object-local surface points uzu_{z} (collision surfaces for DexYCB; visual surfaces for EBench):

(A1) st,zkp=Rtuz+pt,gzkp=Rguz+pg,ft,z=[st,zkp,gzkp,gzkp−st,zkp]∈ℝ9.\begin{gathered}s_{t,z}^{\rm kp}=R_{t}u_{z}+p_{t},\qquad g_{z}^{\rm kp}=R_{g}u_{z}+p_{g},\\ f_{t,z}=[s_{t,z}^{\rm kp},\ g_{z}^{\rm kp},\ g_{z}^{\rm kp}-s_{t,z}^{\rm kp}]\in\mathbb{R}^{9}.\end{gathered}

Point indices define current/goal correspondence. The actor receives these paired features; its LSTM supplies temporal context.

A.2. Retargeting, Filtering, and Resets

  • •

    Retargeting: PyRoki jointly optimizes Sharpa hand joints and root poses over each sequence. Robotiq uses an analytical hand-to-gripper mapping. cuRobo solves collision-aware arm IK with the hand fixed, including the robot and table/workstation geometry and a home-to-first-target approach segment.

  • •

    Contact objective: squared residuals et,j=5​mt,j​[|ct,j−xt,j|−0.01]+e_{t,j}=5m_{t,j}[|c_{t,j}-x_{t,j}|-0.01]_{+}, with componentwise deadband in meters and validity mask mt,jm_{t,j}. Other residual multipliers are listed below.

  • •

    Filtering: we hold IK-valid configurations at their initial joint targets with gravity disabled, and reject states that terminate, produce non-finite measurements, or violate the thresholds below. Final gates test the last sample; peak gates test the entire window. Both Sharpa embodiments share settings.

  • •

    Sampling: each environment retains an assigned object/demo. With probability pp, sample uniformly among its retained frames and use that frame’s robot/object state with the demonstration’s terminal object goal. Otherwise use the home robot configuration and demonstrated object start. Human-derived training uses p=0.9p=0.9 unless ablated; synthetic EBench training uses p=0p=0.

Retargeting parameter Value
Local / global alignment multiplier 10 / 1
Joint / root-translation smoothness 2 / 2
Joint-limit / rest-pose multiplier 100 / 0.2
Arm IK seeds 64
Wrist position / rotation tolerance 5 mm / 0.05 rad
Reset-filter parameter Sharpa / Robotiq
Hold-target steps (30 Hz) 24 / 120
Final object linear speed (m/s) 0.5 / 0.5
Final object angular speed (rad/s) 15 / 15
Final maximum joint speed (rad/s) 10 / 10
Peak object linear speed (m/s) Off / 1.0
Peak gripper-joint speed (rad/s) Off / 2.0

A.3. Rewards

We adopt several reward terms from (Kuang et al., 2026). Let d=dkp​(stkp,gkp)d=d_{\rm kp}(s_{t}^{\rm kp},g^{\rm kp}), PP be the sum of fingertip distances to the nearest object surface keypoints, and MM the analogous palm distance (all in meters). The object-only reward terms are

(A2) rprox\displaystyle r_{\rm prox} =−2.5​min⁡(P,3)−2.5​min⁡(M,0.5),\displaystyle=-2.5\min(P,3)-2.5\min(M,0.5),
G\displaystyle G =𝟙{P≤0.6∧M≤0.2},\displaystyle=\mathds{1}\{P\leq 0.6\ \land\ M\leq 0.2\},
rreorient\displaystyle r_{\rm reorient} =3​(1.4−3​d),\displaystyle=3(1.4-3d),
rsuccess\displaystyle r_{\rm success} =151+10​d𝟙{d≤0.02}.\displaystyle=\frac{15}{1+10d}\mathds{1}\{d\leq 0.02\}.

The geometric gate G=𝟙proxG=\mathds{1}_{\rm prox} multiplies the two goal terms. For clipped actions 𝐚¯t∈[−1,1]na\bar{\mathbf{a}}_{t}\in[-1,1]^{n_{a}} and Δ​𝐚¯t=𝐚¯t−𝐚¯t−1\Delta\bar{\mathbf{a}}_{t}=\bar{\mathbf{a}}_{t}-\bar{\mathbf{a}}_{t-1},

(A3) rsmooth=\displaystyle r_{\rm smooth}={} −0.005​‖𝐚¯t‖22−0.05​‖Δ​𝐚¯tarm‖22\displaystyle-0.005\|\bar{\mathbf{a}}_{t}\|_{2}^{2}-0.05\|\Delta\bar{\mathbf{a}}^{\rm arm}_{t}\|_{2}^{2}
−0.005​‖Δ​𝐚¯thand‖22.\displaystyle-0.005\|\Delta\bar{\mathbf{a}}^{\rm hand}_{t}\|_{2}^{2}.

Safety penalties are −500-500 each for an out-of-bounds object and terminal robot–environment contact (any configured arm/hand sensor above 5 N for 0.5 s). No dense contact penalty is used. The environment multiplies weighted rewards by Δ​t=1/30\Delta t=1/30 s; PPO additionally scales rewards by 0.01, unlike the reported environment return.

Hand-object variant. Object-local fingertip targets cfc_{f} come from the last valid IK frame and follow the current object pose, c~t,f=Rt​cf+pt\tilde{c}_{t,f}=R_{t}c_{f}+p_{t}. Replace rproxr_{\rm prox} by −2.5​min⁡(∑f‖xt,f−c~t,f‖2,3)-2.5\min(\sum_{f}\|x_{t,f}-\tilde{c}_{t,f}\|_{2},3) and GG by a mean fingertip-to-target distance threshold of 0.05 m. Other terms are unchanged; targets specify a grasp region, not a time-indexed trajectory.

A.4. Policy and Training

The actor observes joint positions, controller targets, fingertip-to-object geometry, and paired point features. The critic additionally observes clean geometry, joint/object velocities, goal error, closest-fingertip information, contacts, reward state, and perturbations. UR7e+Sharpa has 648 pre-encoder observations and 28 actions; dimensions vary by embodiment.

Setting Value
PointNet MLP / pooling →→→1289\!\to\!64\!\to\!128\!\to\!128 / max
Actor LSTM / ELU MLP 1 layer, 512 units, layer norm / [512,256,128][512,256,128]
Critic LSTM / ELU MLP 512 units / [512,512,256][512,512,256]
Action head Gaussian; state-independent log std.
Implementation RL Games PPO
Discount / GAE / PPO clip 0.99 / 0.95 / 0.2

Reward scale / gradient cap 0.01 / 1.0

Input / value / advantage normalization Enabled
Observation history / episode limit 1 / 12 s
Physics / policy frequency 120 / 30 Hz

Control. Actions increment persistent joint-position targets. UR7e arm increment/velocity-limit scales are 0.0125/0.2; Sharpa uses increment scale 1/241/24, 90% joint ranges, and effort scale 0.75. Other embodiments use their own controllers/output heads.

Budgets. Each seed (42/52/62) trains on a single GPU. Reported checkpoints are at 10k epochs. Fine-tuning uses 5k DexYCB + 5k EBench epochs; scratch uses 10k EBench epochs, matched within each seed.

Arm / hand transport delay 0–6 / 0–16 physics steps
Perception / proprioception delay 0–6 / 0–1 policy steps

Disturbances. While the proximity gate is active, random-direction object forces satisfy ‖F‖≤150​m\|F\|\leq 150m N (mass mm in kg); arm pushes are bounded by 600 N. Spin impulses use |Δ​ω|≤30|\Delta\omega|\leq 30 rad/s, converted to torque using inertia and the physics timestep. Per-environment event probabilities are log-uniform in [0.001,0.1][0.001,0.1].

A.5. Evaluation

Success is 𝟙{mintdkp(stkp,gkp)≤0.02m}\mathds{1}\{\min_{t}d_{\rm kp}(s_{t}^{\rm kp},g^{\rm kp})\leq 0.02\,\mathrm{m}\} over the rollout, independent of the reward gate and including initially near-goal cases. Episode returns use default resets. Simulation plots show mean ±\pm SE over three training seeds, with SE=std⁡(μ1,μ2,μ3)/3\mathrm{SE}=\mathrm{std}(\mu_{1},\mu_{2},\mu_{3})/\sqrt{3} (sample std.). Object averages are computed within each seed before aggregation.

Study Protocol
DexYCB 20 objects ×\times 20 demonstrated start/goal pairs; 400 pairs per embodiment. Easy/Medium/Hard: 7/7/6; objects weighted equally.
EBench 12 objects (4 per difficulty), used for both fine-tuning/scratch training and evaluation. Zero-shot policies exclude EBench training.
Goal families Lift, 60∘60^{\circ} yaw, 60∘60^{\circ} x-tilt, 60∘60^{\circ} y-tilt; 20 pairs each.
Trials 80 pairs ×\times 5 deterministic draws = 400/object; 4,800/policy/seed, 14,400 across seeds.
Start offsets XY ±0.02\pm 0.02 m; yaw ±25∘\pm 25^{\circ}; seed base 42.
Goal offsets XY ±0.03\pm 0.03 m; yaw ∼±30∘\sim\!\pm 30^{\circ}; Z ±0.05\pm 0.05 m; seed base 71.
Physical 10 attempts/object; grasp and reorientation counts use all attempts (Fig. 7).

EBench Easy: two different soaps, bookmark, mug; Medium: apple, perfume, remote, detergent; Hard: can, mug, fork, bowl. Evaluation perturbation seeds are distinct from training seeds.

A.6. Offline Hand-Pose Noise

Before retargeting/filtering, translate the whole hand by one uniformly sampled wrist offset per demonstration. Add palm-frame finger-keypoint noise with eight-frame correlation, et=ρ​et−1+1−ρ2​σ​εte_{t}=\rho e_{t-1}+\sqrt{1-\rho^{2}}\sigma\varepsilon_{t}, ρ=e−1/8\rho=e^{-1/8}, εt∼𝒩⁡(0,I)\varepsilon_{t}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I), and e0∼𝒩⁡(0,σ2​I)e_{0}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}I). Clip vector norms, rotate to world coordinates, and restore bone lengths; caps apply before restoration. Object poses and untracked sentinel frames remain unchanged.
